title: Solved by walking
hook: a Latin saying, later attached to Diogenes: it is solved by walking

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five remembrances, ending with the one thing you own. Your line was my actions are my own. What did you choose on purpose? Day one hundred twenty-nine.

An hour on the same problem, and nothing. The email you can't word. The decision about the job, the move, the conversation. You've made lists. You've asked three friends. Your head feels like a room with the windows shut. Then you give up, go for a walk to buy milk, and somewhere around the second corner the answer just, sort of, arrives. As if it was waiting for your legs. People have noticed this for a very long time, long enough to give it a Latin name. A new week starts today: walking, the body, and sleep. And it starts with two Latin words. Today's word is solvitur ambulando.
screen: `STUCK FOR AN HOUR.` → `A WALK FOR MILK.` → `THE ANSWER ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Solvitur ambulando means it is solved by walking. The story it's attached to is older than the phrase. In ancient Greece, the philosopher Zeno of Elea built famous puzzles meant to show that motion is impossible: to cross a room, you must first cross half of it, and half of that half, forever, so how do you ever arrive? The story goes that when someone argued this to Diogenes the Cynic, he didn't answer. He stood up and walked around. Diogenes Laertius, a biographer writing long afterward, tells a version of it. The Latin tag came much later again, and people have pinned it on Diogenes ever since. Diogenes spoke Greek, so the Latin words were never his. But the idea caught on, and it grew. Some philosophers took long walks to think. Nietzsche wrote that only thoughts that come from walking have any value. And modern science has poked at it too. In a 2014 Stanford study, people came up with more creative ideas while walking than while sitting, even walking on a treadmill facing a blank wall. It was a lab task, not a life decision, so it's a clue, not a promise. Still, notice what walking does. It moves the body, so the mind loosens its grip. It gives your eyes something new every few steps. And it sets a gentle rhythm, left, right, that your thoughts can ride on. Sometimes you don't solve it. You walk it.
screen: `IT IS SOLVED BY WALKING.` · `DIOGENES STANDS UP AND WALKS.` · `A LATIN TAG, ADDED LATER.` · `THE 2014 STANFORD WALKERS.` · then, large: `WALK IT OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one question to walk with. Settle first. Let one question come up, something real you've been chewing on. Say it once, clearly, inside. Then set it down, the way you'd put a bag on the floor. Feel your feet. Picture your walk later today, ten minutes, the question riding along but not driving. For now, just breathe with it nearby. The bell holds the time.
Solvitur ambulando. Latin for it is solved by walking, a saying pinned on Diogenes, who answered an argument by getting up and moving. Today's word.
Your line: walk it out. Today, take a ten-minute walk with your one question. Don't force an answer; just let it walk beside you. Day one hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Writers, philosophers and plenty of others take a walk to think a problem through, and the Latin phrase solvitur ambulando is sometimes quoted to describe it.

fork.setup: you're Diogenes. someone argues, cleverly, that motion is impossible. what do you do?
fork.reveal: in the story he says nothing and walks. the answer to an argument about motion is to move.

original.note: Latin: it is solved (solvitur) by walking (ambulando). a later tag, not Diogenes' own words; he spoke Greek.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fancy way of saying go for a walk.
what it means: some problems loosen when the body moves, so walk with them.
what a scholar hears: the reply to Zeno's paradoxes of motion; Diogenes Laertius tells of Diogenes answering by walking, and the Latin tag was attached much later.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: SERIOUS count fix: the hook said 'three Latin words'; solvitur ambulando is two. Hook no longer opens 'You know the feeling'; the garbled 'the sources simply don't reach that far' replaced with the plain point that Diogenes spoke Greek; 'centuries later' and 'philosophers took long walks' softened.
Confirm Diogenes Laertius 6.39 as the passage where Diogenes answers an argument against motion by walking about; some sources attribute the tag to Augustine or others instead.
Nietzsche's line paraphrased ('only thoughts reached by walking have value'); confirm section numbering (Maxims and Arrows 34).
Oppezzo & Schwartz 2014: confirm the treadmill-facing-a-wall detail and that the measure was creative idea generation (alternate uses).
Pronunciation given in classical style; ecclesiastical Latin would say SOL-vee-toor.
